title: Ye Servants of God, Your Master Proclaim
author: Charles Wesley
authorBio: Charles Wesley (1707–1788) was an English Anglican priest, co-founder of Methodism, and author of over 6,500 hymns that gave voice to the 18th-century evangelical revival. Traveling across Britain amid fierce opposition, he turned Scripture into courageous congregational praise.

scriptures.passageText: And they cried out in a loud voice: "Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb."
scriptures.theme: Salvation to God Who Sits on the Throne
scriptures.relevance: Stanzas 5 and 6 directly quote this heavenly doxology, lifting persecuted believers' eyes from earthly mobs to the throne of the Lamb.

scriptures.passageText: The seas have lifted up, Lord, the seas have lifted up their voice... Mightier than the thunder of the great waters... the Lord on high is mighty.
scriptures.relevance: Directly inspires stanzas 2 and 4, comparing violent human opposition to roaring ocean waves that cannot overcome the Lord who rules on high.

originalLyrics:
Ye servants of God, your Master proclaim,
And publish abroad His wonderful Name;
The Name all victorious of Jesus extol,
His kingdom is glorious and rules over all.

The waves of the sea have lift up their voice,
Sore troubled that we in Jesus rejoice;
The floods they are roaring, but Jesus is here;
While we are adoring, He always is near.

When devils engage, the billows arise,
And horribly rage, and threaten the skies:
Their fury shall never our steadfastness shock,
The weakest believer is built on a rock.

God ruleth on high, almighty to save,
And still He is nigh, His presence we have;
The great congregation His triumph shall sing,
Ascribing salvation to Jesus, our King.

"Salvation to God, who sits on the throne!"
Let all cry aloud and honor the Son;
The praises of Jesus the angels proclaim,
Fall down on their faces and worship the Lamb.

Then let us adore, and give Him His right,
All glory and power, all wisdom and might,
All honor and blessing, with angels above,
And thanks never ceasing, and infinite love.
contemporaryStanzas: Servants of God, proclaim your Master,
And declare His wonderful Name far and wide;
Exalt the all-victorious Name of Jesus—
His kingdom is glorious and rules over all.
The raging waves of the sea have lifted up their voice,
Deeply angered that we rejoice in Jesus;
The floods are roaring, yet Jesus is right here;
While we worship Him, He is always near.
When hostile powers attack and the storms rise high,
Raging fiercely and threatening the skies,
Their fury will never shake our steadfast faith—
Even the weakest believer stands built on a rock.
God reigns on high, almighty to save,
And still He is close—we have His presence with us;
The great assembly will sing of His victory,
Giving all salvation's praise to Jesus our King.
'Salvation belongs to God, who sits on the throne!'
Let everyone cry aloud and honor the Son;
The angels proclaim the praises of Jesus,
Falling down on their faces to worship the Lamb.
So let us adore Him and give Him what is rightfully His:
All glory and power, all wisdom and strength,
All honor and blessing, joined with angels above,
With gratitude that never ends and boundless love.
hymnBackground: Published in 1744 in Wesley's booklet 'Hymns for Times of Trouble and Persecution' under the remarkable heading 'To be sung in a tumult,' this hymn was written while England feared a French invasion and angry mobs falsely accused Methodists of treason, attacking preachers with stones. Wesley anchored his persecuted flock in Psalm 93 and Revelation 7, pairing their defiance with William Croft's triumphant tune 'HANOVER' (1708).

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: publish abroad His wonderful Name
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: declare His wonderful Name far and wide
lyricInsights.meaning: 'Publish' in 18th-century English meant to announce publicly—an act of bold witness even when mobs threatened Methodist gatherings.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: The waves of the sea have lift up their voice
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: The raging waves of the sea have lifted up their voice
lyricInsights.meaning: Quotes Psalm 93:3 directly; Wesley uses roaring seas as a vivid metaphor for hostile crowds 'sore troubled' by Christian joy.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: The weakest believer is built on a rock
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Even the weakest believer stands built on a rock
lyricInsights.meaning: Echoes Matthew 7:24–25—steadfastness comes not from the believer's personal strength, but from the Rock beneath their feet.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: God ruleth on high, almighty to save
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: God reigns on high, almighty to save
lyricInsights.meaning: Holds together God's transcendence ('on high') and His nearness ('still He is nigh') in a single comforting couplet.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: Fall down on their faces and worship the Lamb
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Falling down on their faces to worship the Lamb
lyricInsights.meaning: Directly echoes Revelation 7:10–11, uniting the persecuted earthly church with the triumphant worship of heaven.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: give Him His right ... thanks never ceasing
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: give Him what is rightfully His ... gratitude that never ends
lyricInsights.meaning: Paraphrases Revelation 7:12's sevenfold doxology (glory, power, wisdom, might, honor, blessing, thanks), concluding the hymn in eternal adoration.

youtubeSources.title: Ye Servants Of God (Hymn 358) | An Evening of Hymns With Men of The Word
youtubeSources.summary: Stirring congregational rendition of Charles Wesley's 1744 anthem of courage sung to William Croft's 'Hanover.'

title: Yield Not to Temptation
author: Horatio R. Palmer
authorBio: Horatio Richmond Palmer (1834–1907) was an American composer, choir director, music theorist, and dean of the Chautauqua School of Music born in Sherburne, New York. Author of influential music textbooks and over 50 song collections, he trained generations of church musicians across the United States.

scriptures.passageText: God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.
scriptures.relevance: Grounds the hymn's confident refrain that believers never face temptation alone—Christ Himself is faithful to carry us through.

scriptures.passageText: Blessed is the one who perseveres under trial because, having stood the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love Him.
scriptures.theme: To Him That O'ercometh, God Giveth a Crown
scriptures.relevance: Directly echoed in stanza 3's promise of a victor's crown for those who persevere through faith.

contemporaryStanzas: Do not give in to temptation, for giving in is sin;
Every victory you win will strengthen you to win the next;
Press forward with courage, master dark impulses,
Keep looking to Jesus—He will carry you through.
Ask the Savior to help you,
To comfort, strengthen, and guard you;
He is always willing to aid you,
He will carry you through.
Turn away from harmful company and reject coarse speech,
Hold God's Name in reverence and never use it carelessly;
Be thoughtful and sincere, kindhearted and faithful,
Keep looking to Jesus—He will carry you through.
Ask the Savior to help you,
To comfort, strengthen, and guard you;
He is always willing to aid you,
He will carry you through.
To everyone who overcomes, God promises a crown;
Through faith we will prevail, even when we feel knocked down;
The One who is our Savior will renew our strength;
Keep looking to Jesus—He will carry you through.
Ask the Savior to help you,
To comfort, strengthen, and guard you;
He is always willing to aid you,
He will carry you through.
hymnBackground: Written and composed in 1868 while Palmer was working on a dry music-theory manuscript, a melody and lyric line suddenly flashed across his mind, compelling him to set aside his textbook and draft the hymn immediately. First published in the 'National Sunday School Teachers' Magazine' (1868), its encouraging chorus—'Ask the Savior to help you'—made it a staple for youth, revivals, and personal perseverance.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: Yield not to temptation, for yielding is sin
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Do not give in to temptation, for giving in is sin
lyricInsights.meaning: Makes a vital biblical distinction: being tempted is not itself sin (even Jesus was tempted, Hebrews 4:15); yielding to it is.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: Ask the Savior to help you ... He is willing to aid you
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Ask the Savior to help you ... He is always willing to aid you
lyricInsights.meaning: Shifts the hymn from moral willpower to grace—victory comes by asking a willing Savior for daily strength.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: bad language disdain ... nor take it in vain
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: reject coarse speech ... never use it carelessly
lyricInsights.meaning: Connects everyday speech and friendships (1 Corinthians 15:33; Exodus 20:7) with authentic reverence for God.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: To him that o'ercometh, God giveth a crown
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: To everyone who overcomes, God promises a crown
lyricInsights.meaning: Echoes Revelation 2:10 and James 1:12, reassuring believers that being 'often cast down' (2 Corinthians 4:9) does not mean defeat.

youtubeSources.title: 🎵 Yield Not To Temptation || Know Your Hymnwriters || Horatio R. Palmer
youtubeSources.summary: Biographical overview of music educator Horatio R. Palmer and the 1868 inspiration behind 'Yield Not to Temptation.'

title: Zion Stands with Hills Surrounded
author: Thomas Kelly
authorBio: Thomas Kelly (1769–1855) was an Irish evangelical preacher, scholar, and prolific hymnwriter born in Dublin, the son of an Irish judge. Trained in law before his conversion and Anglican ordination in 1792, he later built independent congregations across Ireland after church authorities restricted his evangelical preaching, penning 765 scripturally rich hymns including 'The Head That Once Was Crowned with Thorns.'

scriptures.passageText: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the Lord surrounds His people both now and forevermore.
scriptures.relevance: Provides the opening image of stanza 1, comparing Jerusalem's encircling hills to God's unbreakable protection around His people.

scriptures.passageText: Can a mother forget the baby at her breast and have no compassion on the child she has borne? Though she may forget, I will not forget you!
scriptures.relevance: Directly echoed in stanza 2 ('Mothers cease their own to cherish... But no changes can attend Jehovah's love').

scriptures.passageText: The Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.
scriptures.relevance: Supplies the hymn's radiant closing line, assuring refined believers of God's permanent, illuminating presence.

contemporaryStanzas: Zion stands surrounded by protective hills,
Zion, guarded by divine power;
All her enemies will be put to shame,
Even if the whole world unites against her:
Blessed Zion,
What a favored place belongs to you!
Every earthly bond may eventually fail;
Even close friends may prove unfaithful;
Even mothers might forget to care for their own;
Heaven and earth themselves will pass away;
Yet no change
Can ever touch the Lord's unfailing love.
God may test you in the refining furnace,
Only to bring you out shining brighter,
Yet He can never stop loving you;
You are deeply precious in His sight:
God is with you—
God, your everlasting light.
hymnBackground: Published in the 1806 second edition of Kelly's 'Hymns on Various Passages of Scripture,' this steadfast anthem paraphrases Psalm 125:2, Isaiah 49:15, and Isaiah 60:19–20 to reassure God's people of His unshakable covenant protection. Over the 19th century it became widely loved across Protestant traditions—most often sung to Thomas Hastings's bold tune 'ZION' (1830).

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: Zion, kept by power divine ... favored lot
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Zion, guarded by divine power ... favored place
lyricInsights.meaning: 'Zion' symbolizes the Church—God's redeemed people; 'lot' means heritage or portion (Psalm 16:5–6), kept secure even against combined opposition.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: Mothers cease their own to cherish
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: Even mothers might forget to care for their own
lyricInsights.meaning: Paraphrases Isaiah 49:15 to show that even if the strongest human bond fails, God's covenant love remains immutable.

lyricInsights.originalPhrase: In the furnace God may prove thee
lyricInsights.modernPhrase: God may test you in the refining furnace
lyricInsights.meaning: 'Prove' means refine and purify like gold in a crucible (Isaiah 48:10; 1 Peter 1:7)—trials never signal God's abandonment, but His purifying love.

youtubeSources.title: Zion Stands With Hills Surrounded (Zion)
youtubeSources.summary: Traditional hymnal accompaniment of Thomas Kelly's 1806 text set to Thomas Hastings's classic tune 'Zion.'
